# SK2172 — The `!` before `is` reads as a negated `is`

<!-- Generated from Rules/Rikarin.Skala.Rules.Metadata/rules.json. Do not edit. -->

A null-forgiving `!` stands immediately before an `is`, where it suppresses nothing and where the two tokens read as an inverted type test.

| | |
|---|---|
| Category | Correctness |
| Default severity | warning |
| Scope | Semantic |
| Needs a compilation | yes |
| Fix | no |
| Language version floor | — |
| Since | 2.0 |
| ReSharper | `SuppressNullableWarningExpressionAsInvertedIsExpression` (`resharper_suppress_nullable_warning_expression_as_inverted_is_expression_highlighting`) |

## Why

`x! is string` and `!(x is string)` differ by the position of one character and answer opposite questions, and the first is the one that compiles silently in every context. ⚠ **The `!` is doing nothing there, and that is measured rather than argued.** `is` never issues a nullability warning about its own operand — a pattern match is exactly the test that makes a null operand safe — so there is no warning for the `!` to suppress. A probe compiled both spellings under `#nullable enable`: `if (s! is object) { }` followed by `s.Length` reports `CS8602`, and so does the same code with the `!` removed, at the same position. ⚠ **That refutes the reason this rule was first going to ship a fix.** The suppression was assumed to carry forward into the flow state, making its removal unsafe; it does not, and the fix is fixless for the other reason instead — the repair is a guess about which program was meant.

## Example

Instead of:

```csharp
if (value! is string) { Handle(value); }
```

Write:

```csharp
if (value is not string) { Handle(value); }

// or, if the test really was meant to be positive, written without the `!` that does nothing:
if (value is string) { Handle(value); }
```

## When it does not fire

⚠ **Disjoint from `SK2111` by construction rather than by filter, which is why this rule is `Semantic` at all.** `SK2111` reports a `!` that suppresses nothing because nullable *warnings* are switched off at that position, or because the operand is a non-nullable value type; this rule declines both, so no `!` can be reported twice and neither rule needs to know about the other's message. What is left is the case `SK2111` deliberately does not reach: warnings on, a reference or nullable-value operand, and a `!` that is inert because of where it stands rather than because of what it stands on. ⚠ **Only a `!` that is the whole left operand of the `is`.** `list![0] is string` suppresses a real warning on `list` and is not this shape; `text!.Trim() is { Length: > 0 }` suppresses a real dereference warning and is not either. ⚠ **`(x!) is string` is declined**, and the parentheses are the reason: they say which operand the `!` binds to, which is the entire thing the reader of the bare form cannot see. Both the pattern form `x! is T t` and the type-test form `x! is T` are examined, because the parser gives them different node kinds and the reader cannot tell them apart. An operand whose type does not resolve is declined. There is no fix: `x is not T` and `x is T` are both plausible readings of `x! is T` and they are opposite programs, so an automatic repair would be the tool choosing which bug it found. Generated code is excluded.
